title: Why is Public Discourse so Hard?
description: Close to a decade ago, a dear friend of mine talked me into joining an important committee at the school our kids then attended. She said she foresaw difficult discussions coming our way, and she wanted more people on the committee who were able to keep their heads in heated discussions and share careful, calm reasoning. Let’s call her Huldah , after the Old Testament prophetess who saw what was to come. I’m a Philosophy professor who studies virtue in the Christian intellectual tradition. That means that my job, as philosopher, has me disagreeing cordially all day long, and the content of my research has me thinking through how to do that well. So, she didn’t misfire when she asked me to join the committee. And yet, I was hardly prepared for the crowded, acrid meetings that came to pass. Nicolas Andrre Monsiaux, “The Debate of Socrates and Aspasia,” via Wikimedia Commons , 1801. While there were reasonable, understanding people on both sides of the debate, they were the minority. One woman used her thumb and pointer finger to mimic shooting herself in the head when she disliked points being made. Others emphatically rolled their eyes, sneered, chortled, or groaned. Folks would use their allotted time to snootily express platitudes, as if a tautology would prove a substantive policy point, or to aggressively shout assertions, as if disdain or force were the main methods of discussion. And, of course, the worst actors on either side agitated the more moderate members of the other. When it came to respectful and charitable discussion, to flip the phrase, the whole was worse than its parts. The whole process was ugly, and it tore apart a community that otherwise had been healthy and vibrant. The culture of the place changed drastically.

title: Justification: What Must I Do To Be Saved?
description: By Fr. Basil Cole, O.P., and Fr. John Baptist Ku, O.P. Caravaggio, “The Calling of Saints Peter and Andrew,” 1603, via Wikimedia Commons. The Question of Justification The question, “what must I do to be saved,” was posed by the rich young man in Matthew 19:16 (and Mark 10:17), as well as by the suicidal jailer in Acts 16:30. In reply, Jesus and Paul, respectively, do not say, “nothing, God will do it all.” Jesus says, “keep the commandments” and “go, sell what you possess . . . and come, follow me” (19:17, 21). And Paul says, “believe in the Lord Jesus.” But does that mean that I save myself, or that I at least meet God halfway? No. Earning eternal life is infinitely above the natural powers of man. But then, have I no part in my own salvation? At the Final Judgment, will God be judging himself since my actions are completely irrelevant to salvation? Even if I actually do evil things, if I have no free will to choose good versus evil, I will be like an irrational animal just following my instincts. And although we might be enraged at a fox that kills our chickens, we don’t blame the fox as if he were committing a sin. So, how should we understand our being rescued from sin and justified by God? Fortunately, St. Thomas Aquinas addresses this issue in question 113 of the first part of the second part of the Summa Theologiae. Aquinas divides the Summa Theologiae into three parts: (1) on God as he is in himself, (2) on rational creatures’ movement toward God, and (3) on Christ, man’s way back to God. The second part is itself divided into two parts: (1) on anthropology (man’s nature and end, and virtue in general) and (2) on specific virtues. At the end of the first section of the second part, Aquinas treats of grace, which was only implicit in the previous articles.

title: The Greatness of Humility
description: What is humility? Now humility makes a man a good subject to ordinance of all kinds and in all matters; while every other virtue has this effect in some special matter. Therefore after the theological virtues, after the intellectual virtues which regard the reason itself, and after justice, especially legal justice, humility stands before all others. ( ST.II-II.Q161.A5.C (emphasis added). To appreciate the greatness of humility, consider that humility stands before the cardinal virtues of temperance and fortitude . Does not their status as cardinal virtues make them greater than humility? Humility stands before magnanimity and magnificence . How can it be that lowly humility surpasses these virtues of greatness, one of which is even called the crown of the virtues? To answer why humility is so significant , we will first answer: what is humility? Humility is about aspiration for great things, and it has three main elements: a control element, knowledge element, and motivation element. Humility is the virtue by which we control our aspirations for anything we think makes us greater. Aquinas refers to these aspirations with the term hope. Sometimes we need to strengthen these aspirations, but we typically need to restrain them. This act of control is called moderation. We control aspirations in light of self-knowledge, in regards to especially our deficiencies and limitations. We control our aspirations out of divine reverence. We are motivated by divine reverence to act humbly, and this motivation guides us to seek our proper place in God’s providence. Let’s unpack humility’s greatness and these three elements and see why humility is so significant. Thanks for reading Investigations by the Thomistic Institute!
